entry.dc:title: PRODUCTION CAPABILITY OF SURFACE AND UNDERGROUND COAL MINING MACHINERY.
entry.dc:creator: Knight H.E.
entry.dc:description: After a brief review of the United States' past coal output from underground and surface mines, the author discusses the production capabilities of today's mining machines used in conventional underground mining (including continuous mining machines) and in surface mining (including draglines for earth moving). Truck and shovel, scrapers or front-end loaders for overburden removal care not covered. Scheduling, maintenance, government regulations, new technology and some other important factors that influence the production capabilities of underground and surface coal mining machines are analyzed.

entry.dc:title: HEAVY SURFACE EQUIPMENT - INDUSTRY PROBLEMS AND SOLUTIONS.
entry.dc:creator: DeMao P.R.
entry.dc:description: The author discusses a number of problems that the mining industry must deal with in its use of heavy surface mining equipment, and then offers possible solutions to these problems. The paper deals primarily with the largest mobile excavating equipment used in various mining and earthmoving operations in the world today, including walking electric draglines, large stripping and loading shovels, and large blast hole drills. Applications of this equipment in surface coal mining, hard rock minng such as iron, aluminum, copper and other ores, as well as in phosphate mining are examined.

entry.dc:title: RECLAIMING SURFACE MINED LAND IN WEST KENTUCKY.
entry.dc:creator: Powell J.
entry.dc:description: During the 1950s, surface mining of coal in western Kentucky increased to the point that production exceeded that from underground mining. Consequently, the Kentucky general assembly adopted legislation that regulated the surface-mining industry and set particular reclamation standards. This paper presents the current state-of-the-art of reclaiming surface-mined lands in the western Kentucky coal fields. A summary is given of five years of field experimentation and observations made while reclaiming thousands hectares of surface-mined coal spoils in western Kentucky.

entry.dc:title: EFFECTS OF SURFACE MINING UPON SHALLOW AQUIFERS IN THE EASTERN POWDER RIVER BASIN, WYOMING.
entry.dc:creator: Davis R.W.
entry.prism:publicationName: Wyo Univ Water Resour Res Inst Water Resour Ser
entry.dc:description: This is a progress report on activities and results obtained from a continuing monitoring and study program evaluating the effects of surface mining upon shallow aquifers in the AMAX Belle Ayr mine area of the Eastern Powder River Basin. It primarily discusses events during 1976.

entry.dc:title: PHYSICAL PROPERTIES OF WESTERN COAL WASTE MATERIALS.
entry.dc:creator: Backer R.
entry.dc:description: The Bureau of Mines investigated the typical physical and chemical properties of coal waste materials from the western part of the United States. The results are compared, in so far as possible, with the properties of waste materials from eastern coal operations. The authors found a disparity of mines and preparation plants among western U. S. coal operations and dissimilarities with typical operations in the East. The relatively cleaner product from the predominance of surface mining and the occurrence of thicker seams in the West reduces the amount of coal preparation required and the size of the waste piles. Because of the abundance of land available for waste disposal, many of the piles are low and extended over large areas. New concepts relating statistical shear strength data to liquifaction potential are presented. The somewhat limited data indicates that western coal sludge is coarser with higher permeabilities and shear strengths than the eastern deposits.

entry.dc:title: REQUIREMENTS FOR ROLL-OVER PROTECTIVE STRUCTURES AND FALLING OBJECT PROTECTIVE STRUCTURES FOR SURFACE COAL MINES AND SURFACE AREAS OF UNDERGROUND COAL MINES.
entry.dc:creator: Hollop E.
entry.prism:publicationName: US Dep Inter Mesa Inf Rep
entry.dc:description: The adopted standards include regulations currently employed by the Corps of Engineers, Department of Defense, State of California, Occupational Safety and Health Administration, Department of Labor, and the Bureau of Reclamation, Department of Interior. The regulations describe the type of equipment involved, retrofit time table, equipment excluded, Society of Automotive Engineers (SAE) test requirements, and other acceptable effective specifications. The development of MESA's ROPS and FOPS regulations and the appropriate adopted standards are presented in this report. Accident statistics gathered from the mining industry which point out the need for ROPS and FOPS on surface mining equipment are included. Appendices to the report give the adopted standards and MESA's regulations covering ROPS and FOPS.

entry.dc:title: An environmental guide to western surface mining. Part two: impacts, mitigation and monitoring.
entry.dc:creator: Moore R.
entry.dc:description: The manual assembles information about the effects of surface mining in the Western US on fish and wildlife resources and recommends ways to mitigate these effects through carefully planned lease and permit stipulations. Chapter 1 describes the content of the manual and provides guidance to the reader in how to use it most efficiently. Chapter 2 introduces the reader to the regional ecology. The distribution of minerals, and the surface mining techniques likely to be used within the three major geomorphic regions. Chapter 3 provides a detailed list of impact activities associated with surface mining and traces the way in which these activities are evaluated with respect to various ecosystem components. Chapter 4 contains discussions of how the various mine-related effects may be mitigated at high, medium, and low levels of effort. It also provides an evaluation of existing stipulations which have been commonly used toward these same objectives. Chapter 5 contains a conceptual approach to development of a site-specific monitoring program and provides recommendations for monitoring of individual ecosystem components. -from US Govt Reports Announcements, 23, 1979

entry.dc:title: U. S. BUREAU OF MINES MINING RESEARCH PROGRAMMES.
entry.dc:creator: Prast W.
entry.dc:description: The U. S. Bureau of Mines is carrying out a number of mining research programs, the objectives of which are in general to increae efficiency, safety and productivity in U. S. mines - particularly coal mines. In this article details of the various programs currently underway are given, covering almost all aspects of coal mining and including surface mining, oil shale mining and metal/non-metal mining.

entry.dc:title: BUREAU OF MINES OIL SHALE R & D PROGRAM.
entry.dc:creator: Utter S.
entry.dc:description: The Program - Advancing Oil Shale Mining Technology - is part of the Bureau's Energy Research and Development Program that began in 1974. The goals of the program are to (1) provide the technology to produce oil shale/shale oil while maintaining environmental quality, and (2) provide baseline data to assist government and industry in the sound planning and managing of the oil shale resource. The program is divided into Extraction, Environment, Special Studies, and Program Management. The major efforts and hence the major funding are in Extraction and Environment. Under Extraction, studies of surface mining, underground mining, and modified in-situ extraction systems are being conducted. Under Environment, work on waste management is being done. A data bank of all available information about oil shale resources, mining and in-situ extraction systems is being assembled under Special Studies.

entry.dc:title: MATCHING LOADERS AND TRUCKS FOR OPEN PIT MINING
entry.dc:creator: Cummings B.
entry.dc:description: For large scale surface mining operations, a variety of excavating equipment is available for different needs. Each type has its advantages. The power shovel has long life and large capacity. The rubber-tired front end loader has mobility and high cycle rates. To get the best production from any type of equipment requires the proper matching of equipment to the mining operation. The author takes a copper mine as an example.

entry.dc:title: GEORGIA WAY - AN ALTERNATIVE TO DETAILED FEDERAL SURFACE MINING AND LAND RECLAMATION LEGISLATION.
entry.dc:creator: Darby S.
entry.prism:publicationName: Proc Counc Econ AIME Annu Meet
entry.dc:description: Surface mining and land reclamation programs are influenced by many variables, and these primarily determine mineral policies of a particular state or region. The author identifies various factors that can influence the quality of surface mined land reclamation programs and illustrates the desirability of developing, by Congress, flexible, nonrestrictive federal legislation on this subject. The article questions the need for several different federal laws to regulate the various types of surface mining when this can be accomplished with one broad, flexible overall act. An alternate approach for drafting surface mining and land reclamation legislation is suggested.

entry.dc:title: Respiratory status of surface coal miners in the united states
entry.dc:creator: Fairman P.
entry.dc:description: The United States Public Health Service examined 1438 surface coal miners to determine the prevalence of coal workers pneumoconiosis (CWP), chronic bronchitis, and ventnatory impairment among them. Four percent (fifty-nine individuals) owed some roentgen graphic evidence of pneumoconiosis, but only seven miners had films interpreted as CWP of category or greater (according to the UICC/Cincinnati classification system). Moreover, most of the affected miners had worked in underground coal mines for prolonged periods. Significant decrements in pulmonary function to increasing exposure to surface mine dust were demonstrated only in the forced vital capacityof smokers. Increased prevalence of chronic bronchitis with increasing exposure was found in all smoking categories. However, significant airway obstruction was an uncommonimding in nonsmoking miners. Employment in surface mining was not likely to cause either the development of CWP or clinically significant respiratory impairment. © 1977 Taylor & Francis Group, LLC.

entry.dc:title: SAFER AND SPEEDIER HAUL ROADS.
entry.dc:creator: Chironis N.
entry.dc:description: The tonnage capacity and weight of haulage trucks used for surface mining of coal has been climbing rapidly, evolving from the 15 and 20-ton carriers to today's super trucks that can haul as much as 300 tons of coal or overburden. The quality of the haul roads, however, has simply not kept pace with such advancements in truck capacities. The author discusses some new design criteria for haul-road construction that will provide better lines of vision for the vehicle operator, increase the operating speeds of trucks, and reduce haulage costs as well as the number of accidents. Some special safety features for haul roads are also cited.

entry.dc:title: ONAKAWANA LIGNITE DEPOSITS COULD BE USEFUL ENERGY SOURCE FOR ONTARIO.
entry.dc:creator: Anon
entry.dc:description: Onakawana Development Ltd was formed in June 1972. It is a subsidiary of Manalta Coal Ltd, which has six surface mining operations in Alberta and Saskatchewan. The company's proposal for developing a mine at Onakawana is presented.

entry.dc:title: Mined land reclamation in Colorado.
entry.dc:creator: Rold J.
entry.prism:publicationName: Geologic Factors in Land Use Planning House Bill 1041 Proc Govenor S 3rd Conference on Environmental Geology Aspen Co Sept 1975
entry.dc:description: The author effectively refutes three myths about mining in Colorado - that strop mining has scarred a large proportion of the state, that the state has no control over surface mining and it has no control over mining on federal lands in Colorado. Effective use of existing recclamation legislation should provide for multiple-sequential land use for the optimum benefit of the community and the landowner. -Nick Pinder

entry.dc:title: BETTER WAYS TO BUILD HOLLOW FILLS.
entry.dc:creator: Chironis N.
entry.dc:description: Two surface mining techniques rapidly becoming popular in the steep-sloped regions of Appalachia, mountain top removal and contour mining using haulback, are discussed. With these two techniques, the trend is to store initial cuts in the hollows. New specifications that can lead to useful, more stable and less costly fills are explained. Also discussed briefly is a new, possibly better way of removing mountaintops, which involves mining across the ridges.

entry.dc:title: SHOVELS COME BACK IN THE WEST.
entry.dc:creator: Jackson D.
entry.dc:description: Electric power shovels, serving as both stripping and mining units, are making a strong bid to take over a large percentage of the surface mining activities in the West of the U. S. This is especially true in the Powder River Basin of Wyoming and Montana where topography and pit geometry favor the shovel/truck team. The trends in the use of electric power shovels are analyzed, and their economics discussed. Approximately 50% of the medium-size electric power shovels sold this year went to the western coal mines, and 1978 is expected to equal or better that figure.

entry.dc:title: TOTAL UTILIZATION OF A LAND RESOURCE.
entry.dc:creator: Reiss I.
entry.dc:description: Meadowlark Farms pioneered the concept of surface mining as an interim land use. The author elaborates on the concept that coal is a legitimate crop in a long term land use program.

entry.dc:title: MAPCO'S MARTIKI MINES LOOKS FOR FULL PRODUCTION IN 1977.
entry.dc:creator: Anon
entry.dc:description: One of the newest and most modern surface mining operations in the East is gathering steam at Mapco Inc. 's Martiki mine in anticipation of yielding 2. 7 million tons (3 million st) of coal annually. The coal property located in Martin County about 16 km (10 miles) southwest of Inez, Ky. was acquired by Mapco in 1973 from Pocahontas Land Co. , a subsidiary of the Norfolk and Western Railroad. The 73-km**2 (18,000-acre) site is Mapco's first venture in surface mining, although two deep mines have been in operation in western Kentucky since the company entered the coal business in 1971. Using three Marion 201-M 15-m**3 (20-cu yd) shovels, the Martiki mine's production target in 1976 was 1. 5 million tons (1. 7 million st). In 1977, when the full equipment complement of the three 20-cu yd shovels, two 151-M 13-m**3 (15-cu yd) shovels, and a Marion 8200 dragline will be reached, the mine is expected to produce approximately 3 million tons.

entry.dc:title: OIL SANDS IN SITU PROJECTS CONTINUE AT IMPRESSIVE RATE.
entry.dc:creator: Malden M.
entry.dc:description: In-situ research and pilot-plant recovery projects that are aimed at exploiting the massive in-place reserves of Alberta's four major tar sands deposits are reviewed. With reserves estimated at 950 billion bbls of oil in place, the 10. 8 million acres of Athabasca, Cold Lake, Peace River and Wabasea oil sands deposits contain about 74 billion bbls which are covered by less than 150 ft of overburden and thus considered suitable for economic surface mining. The remaining and much bigger part of Alberta's oil sands reserves are covered by a far greater overburden and must be recovered through in-situ recovery techniques.

entry.dc:title: LANDSAT IMAGERY FOR SURFACE-MINE INVENTORY.
entry.dc:creator: Anderson A.
entry.dc:description: A band-ratio method is presented for measuring distributed surface areas proved to be both temporally and geographically extendable. This study has demonstrated the feasibility of strip-mine inventory and monitoring with Landsat multispectral data to within 2 to 3 hectares. The average accuracy of classification is greater than 92 percent for Landsat images from 1973. Using band-ratioing techniques it is possible to extend signatures over a large geographic area and temporally to other Landsat images within the same orbit. The procedures developed are now being incorporated into a comprehensive State monitoring and inventory program to provide, in a rapid and inexpensive manner, accurate inforamtion on the location, size, and condition of areas affected by surface mining.

entry.dc:title: COST MODEL FOR REMOTE INSPECTION OF GROUND SITES.
entry.dc:creator: Maxim L.
entry.dc:description: A simple model is developed to assess the cost/effectiveness of remote sensing for inspection of ground activities with application to the inspection of surface mining operations. The model considers both single and multiple tier systems (those in which additional inspection is conducted if a higher order tier indicates a violation), possible trade-offs between alpha and beta errors, the worth of technological improvement, an certain fixed cost aspects of manned inspection. An interesting conclusion of this analysis is that (with current cost factors) satellite and aircraft inspection systems can be cost/effective even with relatively high (0. 15-0. 25) alpha and beta errors.

entry.dc:title: HOW TO KEEP DIESEL ENGINES AT PEAK EFFICIENCY.
entry.dc:creator: Bly R.
entry.dc:description: Aberrations in the color, pressure and temperature of a diesel engine's exhaust are the symptoms of internal malfunctions, most of which can be easily corrected by regular checks and maintenance, as shown in this article. After suggesting the ways of examining performance and combustion efficiency of modern diesel engines used for surface mining or construction machinery, the author discusses some of the common trouble areas and offers basic guidelines for correcting malfunctions in the air restriction from plugged air cleaners, fuel delivery, valve operations and compression.

entry.dc:title: HAULBACK RECLAIMS NATURALLY.
entry.dc:creator: Anon
entry.dc:description: This article deals with truck haulback which has become a successful technique for surface mining coal throughout the Appalachian regions, and which can tie in naturally and efficiently with land reclamation. The method is likely to meet the two stringent provisions which will probably be included in the federal bill on surface mining: The requirement that surface mined land be returned to the approximate original contour, and the requirement that no spoil be pushed over the mining bench on the slopes below. The single-cut haulback mining method as well as the two-direction haulback method and the multi-seam haulback mining method are highlighted.

entry.dc:title: Control of vibration and noise resulting from surface mine blasting
entry.dc:creator: Kerulis F.
entry.dc:description: After an outline of noise and vibration produced in surface mining, control procedures are outlined. The following reommendations are given. Particle velocities below 2 in. per second greatly reduce the possibility of structural damage as well as noise propagation. Delay caps of greater than eight ms should be used in association with a sequential blasting machine under controlled conditions. Adequate burden and stemming should be utilized to prevent the premature escape of by product gases. Minimization of the height of exposed faces should reduce the effects of air blast caused by face movement. Detonation cord should be buried by one to two ft. of dirt or sand, or low energy detonation cord should be used. Blasting should be restricted if weather conditions are likely to cause down range focusing of air blast waves. Blast frequency should be minimized. Blasting should be timed to coincide with the highest ambient noise level of the immediate area. Notification of residents of blasting times should minimize the element of surprise. Public relations efforts should be increased to educate the general public in blasting procedures and in resultant vibrations and noise effects.
